newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour says budget increases tax burden.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour says budget increases tax burden.

text.p: Main UK opposition Labour party economics spokesman Gordon Brown on Wednesday criticised Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's budget and said it would raise rather than lower the tax burden on voters.

Brown also repeated commitments he said would have been in a Labour budget, including a cut on Value Added Tax on heating bills, a move towards a 10 percent starting rate of income tax and a windfall levy on the profits of privatised utilities.
"Yesterday's budget gave with one hand and then it took away with the other," Brown told the House of Commons during the second day of debate on Tuesday's budget.
Brown added: "What the Chancellor didn't tell you is that after yesterday's budget, you will be paying more tax not less."

Brown repeated figures given by Labour leader Tony Blair on Tuesday, saying that after the budget, the average family would face an additional tax bill of 2,120 pounds compared to what it was paying before the 1992 general election.
Brown said Labour would also make it a priority to cut class sizes in schools and cut National Health Service waiting lists.
It would also be prudent in managing the economy and keep both inflation and interest rates low, Brown said.
